name: Dolor-Vastitas
description: Dolor-Vastitas is a small desert world that embodies desolation, its surface an expanse of rust-colored basalt plains interrupted only by the dried basins of oceans that evaporated millions of years ago. The planet is losing its atmosphere in real time, the thin air measurably thinner with each passing century as solar wind strips molecules from the upper atmosphere faster than geological processes can replace them. The landscape has the feel of slow death, a world not violently destroyed but gradually abandoned by the conditions that once made it viable.

The thin atmosphere carries fine iron oxide dust that tints everything in shades of ochre and rust, settling on every surface in a film that must be constantly cleaned from equipment. Winds are gentle but persistent, redistributing the dust in patterns that create the illusion of movement across an otherwise static landscape. The silence is not absolute but muted, sounds traveling poorly in the thin air, voices carrying a quality of distance even in close conversation. The emotional weight of the place is considerable; survey teams report persistent low mood during surface deployments.

The ruins of an abandoned human settlement in the northern hemisphere tell a more recent story of loss. Founded forty years ago as a mining colony, the settlement was abandoned after the subsurface water reserves proved far smaller than initial surveys indicated. The atmospheric moisture traps installed by the colonists still function, collecting the tiny amounts of humidity from the air with mechanical patience, their reservoirs slowly filling with water that no one will ever drink. The buildings stand empty but intact, preserved by the dry conditions, a ghost town on a ghost world.

Microbial life persists in the subsurface, extremophiles that metabolize iron compounds and survive on traces of water bound in mineral structures. These organisms are among the most resilient life forms known, but even they are declining as the planet's water budget approaches zero. Dolor-Vastitas has become a case study in planetary death, a world that has not yet finished dying, its slow decline offering scientists a real-time view of processes that will eventually claim many currently habitable worlds. The name, meaning vast sorrow, was not assigned lightly.
